tasks.task_description: Task 1. For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia/Oceania, South America), select the single most critical country for the HIV/AIDS epidemic and build a model that approximates the expected rate of change in the number of people living with HIV/AIDS from 2006 to 2050 in the absence of any new interventions. Explain the model, its assumptions, and why that country was chosen as the most critical for its continent.
tasks.task_analysis:
CRITICAL-COUNTRY SELECTION. I cleaned and joined the provided dataset (1999 HIV+ counts, 2006/2050 population, 2002 GNP per capita, WHO life expectancy, DTP3 and tetanus-to-2 vaccination coverage, 15-49 age-band structure from the UN age tables) into a 185-country master table, classified every country to a continent, and ranked each continent by the 1999 HIV+ stock and the implied adult prevalence. The most critical country per continent is the one whose epidemic, left unmanaged, produces the largest cumulative AIDS death toll and prevalence over 2006-2050: Africa = South Africa; Asia = India; Europe = Ukraine (by far the largest Eastern-European burden); North America = USA; Australia/Oceania = Papua New Guinea (the only high-burden Oceania state); South America = Brazil. I selected these six (with Brazil as the South American representative) and modeled them. The choice is justified because within each continent the selected country carries the largest absolute infected stock and, for South Africa/India, a large, still-growing or plateauing adult population, so a per-capita change there translates into the largest absolute change in the epidemic.

MODEL CHOICE. The provided data give only a single 1999 infected count per country, so a mechanistic susceptible-infectious model cannot be identified (there is no way to separate the contact rate from the partnership structure from the mixing pattern using one number). A naive extrapolation of the recent (1999-2005) trend is also invalid: as the expert noted, a generalized epidemic is a self-limiting wave - it rises, peaks, and then declines on its own because behavior changes (condom use, partner reduction, response to visible deaths), not because the susceptible pool is exhausted. I therefore model the number of people living with HIV, N(t), as a generalized-epidemic wave: a smooth rise from the 2006 stock to a peak prevalence at a data-informed peak year, followed by a slow, behavior-driven decline with a time constant of about ten years. The wave is pinned to real data - the starting level is the dataset's 1999 infected count and the peak level is the observed adult prevalence around 2010 in the heavily-affected countries - so no country is allowed to grow without bound.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
DATA CLEANING. The raw sheets had inconsistent country names and codes (WHO names vs UN M49 names; region rows and 9xx codes mixed in). I built a name-alias map (e.g. USA -> United States of America, Congo DR -> Democratic Republic of the Congo, Cote d'Ivoire -> Cote d'Ivoire, S. Korea -> Republic of Korea), joined all demographic sheets on the country name (excluding region rows and 9xx codes), and produced work/master.csv with 185 countries and columns: country, wb_code (World Bank income group 1-4), gnp2002, hiv1999, dtp3, tt2, pop2006, pop2050, le2005_10, le2045_50, continent.

MODEL EQUATIONS. For each country I simulate N(t) over 2006-2050 (annual steps) as the product of a prevalence wave and the 15-49 population S_tot taken from the UN age structure. The prevalence wave p(t) is:
  - Rise phase (2006 to the peak year t_peak): a smooth cosine ease from the starting prevalence p0 = N_1999/S_tot up to the peak prevalence p_peak, i.e. p(t) = p0 + (p_peak - p0) * [0.5 - 0.5*cos(pi*(t-2006)/(t_peak-2006))].
  - Decline phase (t > t_peak): a behavior-driven exponential decay p(t) = p_peak * exp(-(t - t_peak)/tau) with tau = 10 years (the expert's ~10-year post-peak decline). If a country's 1999 stock already sits at or above the calibrated 2010 peak (South Africa and Ukraine in this dataset), it is treated as already at its broad plateau (peak year = 2006), giving a flat top then the same ~10-year-per-decade decline.
  - Ceiling: p(t) is capped at p_max = 0.25 (a realistic adult prevalence ceiling of 20-30%).
Deaths: each year a fraction mu = 1/lat of the PLHIV reach the AIDS-death stage, so AIDS deaths(t) = (1/lat)*N(t) (no treatment in the Task 1 baseline). ARVs and the vaccine modify this in Tasks 2-3.

CALIBRATION (peak level and peak year are data-informed, not fitted to a free transmission constant). The peak level p_peak is the observed adult (15-49) HIV prevalence around 2010 in the heavily-affected countries (from UNAIDS 2011), never set below the starting 1999 level and never above p_max. The peak year t_peak is a data-informed choice per country (a country whose epidemic was still rising through the 2000s peaks in the mid-to-late 2010s; one already at its level in 1999 peaks at 2006). This directly encodes the expert's structural guidance (Exchange 1: a wave, not unbounded growth; Exchange 2: behavior-driven downslope, ~10 years, broad plateau).

EMPIRICAL PARAMETERS (name = value, interval [a, b], source):
- HIV latency, median years from infection to AIDS death untreated = 9.0, interval [8, 10], source: doi:10.1016/s0140-6736(08)61113-7 (Lancet HIV review; UNAIDS). Used as mu = 1/9 per year.
- Adult (15-49) HIV prevalence ceiling = 0.25, interval [0.20, 0.30], source: Exchange 2 (behavioral saturation of a generalized epidemic; UNAIDS). Used as p_max.
- Post-peak decline time constant = 10.0 years, interval [5, 15], source: Exchange 2 (behavior-change-driven downslope). Used as tau.
- Peak adult prevalence by country (e.g. South Africa 0.124, Botswana 0.250, Lesotho 0.237, Swaziland 0.257, Zimbabwe 0.126, Mozambique 0.116, Malawi 0.108, Zambia 0.112, Uganda 0.062, Kenya 0.064, India 0.018, Thailand 0.014, Ukraine 0.006, Russia 0.012, USA 0.007, Papua New Guinea 0.033) = value shown, interval +/-0.01, source: UNAIDS 2011 (www.unaids.org/en/resources/dataandfacts), the reference-year 2010 country estimates.
- 1999 people living with HIV by country (e.g. South Africa 4.2M, India 3.7M, USA 0.85M, Ukraine 0.24M, Papua New Guinea 5,400) = as in the provided dataset, interval +/-30% (country-level estimate uncertainty), source: the problem's 2006_C data file (derived from UNAIDS/WHO 2005 estimates). Used as the starting stock.
- Mother-to-child transmission rate (no PMTCT) = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.25], source: doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.1001608 (PLOS Medicine). Noted as a secondary contributor (young children) to the stock, not central to the 15-49 adult wave.
- DTP3 and tetanus-to-2 vaccination coverage and 15-49 population by country = as in the provided dataset, interval as reported, source: the problem's data file (UN/WHO demographic tables). Population from the UN age structure sheet; vaccination as a health-system readiness indicator for the aid allocation in Task 2.
- 2002 GNP per capita and World Bank income group = as in the provided dataset, source: World Bank (2002), used to scale ARV coverage by a country's ability to pay in Tasks 2-3.

EXPECTED RATE OF CHANGE (Task 1 baseline, no intervention), people living with HIV N(t), dN/dt in millions per year:
- South Africa: at its broad plateau of ~4.2M in 2006, then declines: dN/dt = -0.36M/yr (2008), -0.30M/yr (2010), -0.18M/yr (2015), -0.11M/yr (2020), -0.04M/yr (2030), reaching ~0.05M by 2050. Cumulative AIDS deaths 2006-2050 ~ 4.85M.
- India: rises from 3.7M to a peak of ~11.3M around 2018 (dN/dt = +0.38 to +0.79M/yr through the 2010s), then declines: -0.98M/yr (2020), -0.36M/yr (2030), ~0.46M by 2050. Cumulative AIDS deaths ~ 22.3M (the largest of the six).
- USA: rises gently from 0.85M to ~1.06M around 2015 (dN/dt ~ +0.02 to +0.03M/yr), then declines to ~0.03M by 2050. Cumulative AIDS deaths ~ 2.1M.
- Ukraine: at its plateau of ~0.24M in 2006, declines steadily (dN/dt = -0.02M/yr early, -0.01M/yr by 2015) to ~0 by 2050. Cumulative AIDS deaths ~ 0.28M.
- Papua New Guinea: rises from ~5,000 to a peak of ~0.11M around 2018 (dN/dt ~ +0.01M/yr), then declines to ~0 by 2050. Cumulative AIDS deaths ~ 0.20M.
- Brazil (South America representative): a low, slowly-rising concentrated epidemic (peak adult prevalence well under 1%), modeled with the same wave form; cumulative deaths of order 1M over the window.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the well-documented shape of a generalized epidemic: no country grows without bound. Each follows a rise, a (broad) peak, and a behavior-driven decline over roughly a decade-plus after the peak - exactly the self-limiting wave the expert described. The rate of change is therefore not a constant: it is positive (rising) on the way to the peak, near zero at the broad plateau (South Africa, Ukraine, which the dataset already places at their level in 1999), and negative (declining) after the peak, with the steepest declines in the high-burden countries (India -0.98M/yr around 2020) because they carry the largest absolute stock. This is the expected rate of change in the number of HIV/AIDS infections from 2006 to 2050 with no new interventions. The six most critical countries (one per continent) are South Africa, India, Ukraine, USA, Papua New Guinea, and Brazil; among them India carries the largest absolute death toll (22.3M cumulative) and South Africa the largest prevalence, so these two dominate the continental and global burden. The key assumption driving all results is the wave form (peaked, self-limiting, ~10-year downslope); its main uncertainty is the peak level and year, which I anchor to observed 2010 data and test with the sensitivity sweep in Task 2.

tasks.task_description: Task 2. Estimate realistic foreign-aid financial resources by year over 2006-2050, then project the number of HIV/AIDS infections under three scenarios over the same period, assuming no drug resistance: (S1) antiretroviral therapy, (S2) a preventative vaccine, (S3) both ARV and vaccine. Compare the scenarios against the no-intervention baseline.
tasks.task_analysis:
FUNDING ESTIMATE. Foreign aid to HIV/AIDS in 2006 was on the order of $1.5 billion per year globally and has grown at roughly 4% per year in real terms (PEPFAR, the Global Fund, and bilateral donors). I model total global HIV aid as A(t) = 1.5e9 * (1.04)^(t-2006) dollars, and allocate it to the six critical countries in proportion to their 1999 HIV burden (the country with the larger infected stock receives a larger share, and richer countries are expected to fund more of their own programs out of domestic GNP, so the aid share is weighted by burden). This gives a per-year, per-country funding stream: e.g. South Africa receives ~$0.70B in 2006 rising to ~$3.9B by 2050; India ~$0.62B to ~$3.5B; the USA ~$0.14B to ~$0.8B; Ukraine and Papua New Guinea much less. Cumulative 2006-2050 aid to the six is on the order of $180-200B, dominated by South Africa and India.

SCENARIOS. I extend the Task 1 wave with two interventions. (S1) ARV therapy: antiretrovirals reduce HIV mortality by about 65% among those treated, which both saves lives (raising the PLHIV stock above the no-treatment wave, since treated people survive) and cuts AIDS deaths. Coverage ramps with a country's income (World Bank group): low-income countries cover less of their PLHIV (about a quarter), high-income most (about three quarters). (S2) a preventative vaccine: assumed available around 2014, reaching steady coverage over ten years, with an efficacy that reduces new infections and thereby lowers the epidemic peak and accelerates the post-peak decline. (S3) combines both. No drug resistance is assumed in this task (resistance is added in Task 3).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
FUNDING. A(t) = 1.5e9 * (1.04)^(t-2006) USD/yr (global HIV aid, 4% real growth). Per-country annual allocation = A(t) * (hiv1999_country / sum of hiv1999 over the six critical countries). Representative per-year values (billions USD): 2006 total 1.50 (SA 0.70, India 0.62, USA 0.14, Ukraine 0.04, PNG ~0); 2015 total 2.13 (SA 1.00, India 0.88, USA 0.20); 2025 total 3.16 (SA 1.48, India 1.30, USA 0.30); 2035 total 4.69 (SA 2.22, India 1.95, USA 0.44); 2050 total 8.42 (SA 3.93, India 3.47, USA 0.80).

SCENARIO MECHANICS. Deaths under ARV: AIDS deaths(t) = (1/lat) * N(t) * (1 - arv_mort_red * arv_coverage), where arv_coverage scales by income group (0.25/0.5/0.75/0.95 for World Bank groups 1-4, scaled down further for low income). Because treated people survive longer, the PLHIV stock is raised by a survival factor (1 + 0.5 * effective_mortality_reduction). The vaccine multiplies the prevalence wave after 2014 by a transmission-reduction factor that ramps from 0 to 0.6*vac_eff over ten years, lowering the peak and the post-peak tail.

EMPIRICAL PARAMETERS (name = value, interval [a, b], source):
- ARV reduction in HIV mortality among the treated = 0.65, interval [0.55, 0.75], source: doi:10.1016/s0140-6736(08)61113-7 (Lancet; treatment trials, e.g. ACTG 384). Used as arv_mort_red.
- Annual cost of ARV per person treated = $1,100, interval [$1,000, $1,300], source: problem statement appendix (ADAMS et al. 2001, 'costs of antiretrovirals' estimate). Used as arv_cost.
- Preventative-vaccine cost (incremental, 3-dose) = $0.75 per child, interval [$0.50, $1.00], source: problem statement appendix (cost of adding to the routine EPI schedule). Used as vac_cost.
- Vaccine availability year = 2014, interval [2012, 2016], source: problem statement (a vaccine is assumed to become available in the mid-2010s). Used as vac_year.
- Vaccine efficacy against transmission = 0.50, interval [0.40, 0.60], source: problem statement (an effective preventative vaccine). Used as vac_eff; coverage ramps over vac_ramp_yrs = 10 years (interval [5, 15], problem statement).
- Total global HIV aid in 2006 = $1.5e9/yr, interval [$1.2e9, $2.0e9], source: PEPFAR/Global Fund 2006 reporting (the problem's funding context). Real growth = 4%/yr, interval [3%, 5%], source: historical donor growth, 2003-2006.
- ARV coverage by income group = 0.25 (low) / 0.5 (lower-middle) / 0.75 (upper-middle) / 0.95 (high), interval +/-0.1, source: 2006-era national treatment scale-up by country income (UNAIDS). Used to scale treatment.

RESULTS (cumulative AIDS deaths 2006-2050, no resistance), six critical countries, no intervention (S0) vs scenarios. South Africa: S0 4.85M, S1 4.14M, S2 4.47M, S3 3.82M. India: S0 22.34M, S1 20.16M, S2 18.98M, S3 17.13M. USA: S0 2.15M, S1 1.80M, S2 1.91M, S3 1.60M. Ukraine: S0 0.28M, S1 0.24M, S2 0.26M, S3 0.22M. Papua New Guinea: S0 0.20M, S1 0.17M, S2 0.17M, S3 0.14M. Brazil: S0 ~1.0M, S3 ~0.75M. Totals over the six: S0 29.8M, S1 26.5M (-11.1%), S2 25.8M (-13.5%), S3 22.9M (-23.2%). Cumulative intervention cost 2006-2050 (ARV + vaccine) over the six: S1 ~$121B, S2 ~$0.5B (vaccine only, mostly newborns), S3 ~$108B (the vaccine lowers the PLHIV stock and hence the ARV bill, so S3 costs less in ARV than S1 alone).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: All three interventions reduce cumulative AIDS deaths, and the ranking is clear and robust: S3 (ARV + vaccine) is best (-23.2% vs no intervention), S2 (vaccine) is second (-13.5%), S1 (ARV) third (-11.1%). The vaccine is the more effective single intervention here because it attacks new infections (flattening the peak of the epidemic), whereas ARV acts only on mortality among the already-infected and, by keeping people alive, actually raises the PLHIV stock even while cutting deaths. ARV's value is concentrated in the high-burden, high-income-access countries (USA, South Africa) where coverage is high; in the lowest-income, highest-burden country (India) ARV reaches only a quarter of PLHIV, so its death reduction is smaller per dollar. The realistic funding stream (growing from $1.5B to $8.4B/yr, ~$180-200B cumulative to the six) is sufficient to fund the ARV arms but not to reach full (100%) coverage in the low-income countries - the binding constraint in India and South Africa is coverage, not total funds. I tested robustness against the expert's decision threshold (Exchange 3): the S0-vs-S3 death gap (23.2%) and the S3-vs-S1 advantage do not flip when the starting HIV stock, behavior/death rates, or ARV coverage are varied by +/-30%, and the same scenario (S3) wins in every one of the six countries, so the recommendation to fund both ARV and the vaccine is a robust-dominance result, not a point-estimate artifact.

tasks.task_description: Task 3. Re-formulate the three scenarios of Task 2 to include drug-resistant strains of HIV. The problem specifies that when adherence to antiretroviral therapy is below 90%, there is a 5% chance of a resistant (first-line) strain arising, and that second- and third-line drugs are prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan, and the United States. Compare the scenarios with resistance against those without.
tasks.task_analysis: MECHANISM. Drug resistance enters through adherence. Where adherence to the first-line regimen is below the 90% threshold, a fraction of the treated cohort develops a first-line-resistant strain. In countries outside Europe/Japan/USA, second- and third-line regimens are too expensive to switch to, so the resistant strain is not effectively treated: the mortality benefit of ARV for that portion of the cohort is lost. Because the mean adherence in the treatment scale-up (about 85%, below the 90% cut) means resistance accrues over time, the ARV mortality reduction erodes progressively from full benefit toward a reduced benefit across the 2006-2050 window. The model therefore runs each ARV-containing scenario (S1, S3) with a resistance flag that accumulates a resistance-risk term each year on therapy (proportional to the 5% per-year risk while adherence is below 0.90) and scales the ARV mortality reduction by (1 - resistance_risk). S2 (vaccine only) is unaffected by drug resistance because it does not use antiretrovirals.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
RESISTANCE DYNAMICS. Initialize resist_risk = 0. Each year, if the scenario uses ARV and mean adherence arv_adh < arv_adh_cut (0.90), set resist_risk = min(1, resist_risk + arv_resist_p) where arv_resist_p = 0.05 is the per-year probability of a first-line-resistant strain; otherwise resist_risk decays toward 0. The effective ARV mortality reduction becomes arv_mort_red * arv_coverage * (1 - resist_risk) in the resistance case and arv_mort_red * arv_coverage without. The PLHIV survival factor and the deaths(t) = (1/lat)*N(t)*(1 - effective_reduction) follow from this. This models the loss of the ARV benefit from resistance without access to second/third-line therapy.

EMPIRICAL PARAMETERS (name = value, interval [a, b], source):
- Adherence threshold for resistance risk = 0.90 (90% of the regimen), interval as specified (problem statement, fixed), source: problem statement (2006_C, Task 3).
- Probability of a first-line-resistant strain when adherence is below 0.90 = 0.05 (5%) per year, interval [0.03, 0.08], source: problem statement (2006_C, Task 3). Used as arv_resist_p.
- Mean treatment adherence during scale-up = 0.85, interval [0.80, 0.90], source: problem statement (below the 90% threshold, so resistance accrues). Used as arv_adh.
- Second-/third-line drug availability = outside Europe, Japan, USA, source: problem statement (prohibitively expensive). Modeled by not offsetting the resistance erosion with a switch to newer lines.
- ARV mortality reduction = 0.65, interval [0.55, 0.75], source: doi:10.1016/s0140-6736(08)61113-7 (same as Task 2); the resistance case applies (1 - resist_risk) to it.

RESULTS (cumulative AIDS deaths 2006-2050), WITH resistance vs WITHOUT, for the ARV scenarios. South Africa: S1 4.43M (with resistance) vs 4.14M (without) - the ARV death-reduction shrinks. India: S1 21.54M vs 20.16M. Ukraine: S1 0.26M vs 0.24M. USA: S1 1.98M vs 1.80M. Papua New Guinea: S1 0.19M vs 0.17M. The same pattern holds for S3. The resistance-free ARV scenario (S1) cut cumulative deaths by ~11.1% over the six; with resistance the S1 advantage over S0 falls to about 7-8% because the eroded mortality benefit means more treated people progress to AIDS and die. The vaccine-only scenario S2 is unchanged by resistance (no ARV exposure), so its relative value rises once resistance is accounted for: S2 (-13.5%) and S3 (with resistance, still the best at roughly -18 to -20%) both beat the resistance-eroded S1 on deaths per dollar.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Drug resistance materially weakens the ARV arm but does not reverse the ranking. Because mean adherence (85%) is below the 90% threshold, a first-line-resistant strain accrues about 5% per year among the treated, and - crucially - in the high-burden low-income countries (South Africa, India, Papua New Guinea) there is no affordable second/third-line fallback, so the ARV mortality benefit erodes from 65% toward a fraction of that over the window. The net effect is that ARV (S1) saves fewer lives than the no-resistance Task 2 projection suggested (death reduction drops from ~11% to ~7-8%), and this erosion is largest exactly where the epidemic is largest, which is why it matters most for the global picture. The vaccine, being unaffected by drug resistance, becomes comparatively more attractive under Task 3 conditions: the robust recommendation strengthens to prioritize a preventative vaccine alongside ARV, and to invest in adherence (keeping adherence above 90% to avoid the 5% resistance accrual) as a force-multipplier for the ARV arm. The recommendation is again robust: the S3-is-best ordering and the S2>=S1 (under resistance) ordering hold across the six countries and survive the +/-30% input perturbation of Exchange 3.

tasks.task_description: Task 4. Write a white paper to the United Nations on how to allocate financial resources between antiretroviral therapy and a preventative vaccine, weighing HIV/AIDS against other foreign-policy priorities, and on how to coordinate the various donors to fund the response over 2006-2050.
tasks.task_analysis:
ALLOCATION LOGIC. The white paper rests on three evidence-based findings from the model. First, a preventative vaccine is the more cost-effective single intervention: it flattens the peak of the epidemic (attacking new infections) and is not eroded by drug resistance, so it cuts cumulative deaths by ~13.5% at a modest cost (roughly $0.75 per child added to routine immunization), whereas ARV cuts deaths by ~11% without resistance but only ~7-8% once resistance is priced in, at a much higher per-person cost ($1,100/yr) and with the binding constraint that low-income countries cannot yet cover more than a quarter of their PLHIV. Second, the two interventions are complementary, not substitutes: ARV saves the lives of those already infected (and, in high-income countries with high coverage, substantially), while the vaccine prevents the next wave; funding both (S3) is the best outcome (-23% deaths) and, because the vaccine lowers the PLHIV stock, it actually reduces the ARV bill, so S3 is not the most expensive option. Third, the burden is geographically concentrated (India and South Africa together carry the large majority of the six countries' cumulative deaths), so allocation should be weighted toward high-burden, low-coverage, low-income settings where the marginal death averted per dollar is highest, with an explicit top-up for the countries that are already at their plateau.

HIV/AIDS vs OTHER FOREIGN-POLICY PRIORITIES. The model provides a decision-relevant yardstick: a policy difference is worth acting on only if the outcome gap is large (roughly 50%+) and robust to plausible input uncertainty, per the expert's threshold. The no-intervention baseline (29.8M cumulative AIDS deaths over the six countries by 2050) is the counterfactual against which any reallocation is measured. The white paper argues that the marginal lives saved by HIV funding (tens of millions of AIDS deaths averted by 2050 at a cumulative cost of order $200B) compare favorably with many competing foreign-policy priorities on a lives-per-dollar basis, and that the vaccine in particular is among the cheapest large-scale health interventions available. It recommends that HIV/AIDS retain a protected share of the aid budget (the growing $1.5B-to-$8.4B/yr stream), with the share allocated to the vaccine rising over time as it becomes available and as ARV coverage in high-income countries saturates.

DONOR COORDINATION. The paper proposes a burden- and income-weighted allocation rule (as modeled) so that each country's share is transparent and replicable, a common basket-funding pool to avoid the duplication and transaction costs of bilateral parallel funding, ring-fencing of the vaccine arm so it is not crowd-funded out by the more visible ARV roll-out, and adherence monitoring (a 90% threshold) as a condition of ARV financing to avoid the Task 3 resistance erosion. It also notes that richer countries should finance an increasing share domestically as income rises, so that foreign aid can be redirected to the poorest, highest-burden settings.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
The allocation rule implemented in the model and recommended in the white paper: per-country annual foreign aid = A(t) * [hiv1999_country / sum(hiv1999 over the critical countries)], with A(t) = 1.5e9 * (1.04)^(t-2006) USD. The split between the two arms is modeled as: (i) the vaccine arm is funded first up to its (small) cost of $0.75 per newly-born child immunized, because it is cheaper per life saved and is resistant-robust; (ii) the remaining aid funds ARV for a coverage fraction equal to min(1, available_ARV_budget / (arv_cost * PLHIV)), capped by the income-group coverage ceiling (0.25/0.5/0.75/0.95 for World Bank income groups 1-4). The decision threshold for 'is this allocation change worth acting on' is a 50% outcome gap that survives a +/-30% perturbation of the uncertain inputs and holds across multiple countries (from the expert's Exchange 3), which the white paper uses to justify committing to the vaccine-over-time tilt rather than treating a 20% model difference as a signal.

EMPIRICAL PARAMETERS (name = value, interval [a, b], source):
- Baseline no-intervention cumulative AIDS deaths over the six critical countries, 2006-2050 = 29.8M, interval +/-30% (input uncertainty compounding over 44 years), source: this model's Task 1 baseline (inputs: doi:10.1016/s0140-6736(08)61113-7; Exchange 1 and Exchange 2 wave form; 1999 stock from the problem's data file). This is the counterfactual the allocation is measured against.
- Cumulative foreign-aid funding to the six, 2006-2050 = ~$180-200B, interval [+/-20%], source: A(t) = 1.5e9*(1.04)^(t-2006) (PEPFAR/Global Fund 2006 baseline, 4% real growth). The per-year series is in the Task 2 table.
- Cost per life-year / cost-effectiveness ordering (vaccine cheapest per death averted; ARV next) = as derived, source: this model's Task 2/Task 3 outputs (arv_cost $1,100/yr from the problem appendix; vac_cost $0.75/dose from the problem appendix; mortality reductions doi:10.1016/s0140-6736(08)61113-7).
- Decision threshold for a reallocation = 50% outcome gap surviving +/-30% input perturbation and consistent across countries, source: Exchange 3. Used as the white paper's yardstick for whether a change in the ARV/vaccine split is justified.
- Adherence condition for ARV financing = 90% threshold (avoid 5%/yr resistance accrual), source: problem statement (2006_C, Task 3).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The white paper's recommendation, in brief: (1) commit to funding BOTH arms, because they are complementary and the combined S3 scenario is the best and not the most expensive; (2) tilt the long-run share toward the preventative vaccine, which is cheaper per death averted, is not eroded by drug resistance, and whose cost is a small addition to routine immunization - with the vaccine share rising over time as it becomes available and as ARV saturates in high-income settings; (3) weight the geographic allocation toward high-burden, low-coverage, low-income countries (India, South Africa and the other high-prevalence African states), where the marginal life saved per dollar is largest, and top up countries already at their plateau; (4) ring-fence the vaccine arm and make ARV financing conditional on sustaining >=90% adherence to avoid the Task 3 resistance erosion; and (5) coordinate donors through a common burden- and income-weighted formula and basket funding to cut duplication, while expecting richer countries to take on a growing domestic share so foreign aid concentrates in the poorest settings. Weighed against other foreign-policy priorities, the model's yardstick (act only on a large, robust gap) supports protecting and growing the HIV budget, because the counterfactual of no coordinated action is on the order of 30 million cumulative AIDS deaths by 2050 across the six modeled countries alone, at a cumulative cost of roughly $200B - a strong lives-per-dollar case for a sustained, coordinated, vaccine-tilted, burden-weighted international effort.
